subtype_info: abdominal and splenic hydatidosis simulating acute abdomen
title: Hydatid disease simulating acute abdomen: a case report and brief review of the literature
case_text: A 72-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the emergency department of the University Hospital of Ioannina due to diffuse abdominal pain, nausea and progressively increasing abdominal distension of ten-day duration. His medical history was free and no recent trauma was reported. Clinical examination revealed pyrexia of 38.5 C, tachycardia of 110 per minute, and normal blood pressure. Upon physical examination, a grossly distended and diffusely tender abdomen was revealed. On auscultation abdominal sounds were present. Rectal examination showed an empty rectum. The emergent laboratory tests revealed as follow: WBC 14700 mm3, haemoglobin at 10.5 g/dL, c-reactive protein was at 148 mg/l, creatinine, electrolytes, and liver function tests were normal. The examination of urine was also normal. The abdominal plan X-ray was normal and an urgent abdominal CT was arranged. The CT revealed a huge hepatic hydatid cyst (measuring 14.5 cm) with daughter cysts in the left lobe of the liver and multiple splenic hydatidosis. Additionally, a large echinococcal cyst was revealed at the left hypochondrium attached to the anterior wall of the stomach causing a huge pressure (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). Hydatid cysts were also revealed in the transverse mesocolon and in pelvis. Laparotomy was performed the day after the admission due to progressively increasing abdominal distension and to diffuse abdominal pain. Intraoperative findings confirmed the diagnosis of abdominal and splenic hydatidosis. The patient was treated with deroofing and omentoplasty for the large hepatic echinococcal cyst, splenectomy for the splenic cysts, and removal of the rest echinococcal cysts. The postoperative period was uneventful and the patient was discharged 15 days later, with the advice to receive albendazole for three months postoperatively.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: abdominal and splenic hydatidosis simulating acute abdomen
